title: Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker and the new sound
summary: Dizzy sat in at the Black Cat, Hall knew Parker and Gillespie from Philadelphia and saw bebop as evolution.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: When I was working with Skeets Talbot from club at the Black Cat, Dizzy used to come up to the club and sit
in and make these screaming sounds and they'd chase him out.
Now, you knew him in Philly I guess?

I knew him in Philly. I knew him and I and 'Bama' [Carl WARWICK] Jimmy Hamilton knew Charlie in Philly, yeah, we came up, and --but, this was then a new sound and the guys were jamming at Minton's, but I was working in the studio then.
Yeah.
So, this was a --
So, you weren't into jamming then?
No. Yeah, I was into jamming, we made 'V' discs and things, and visits but my jobs were always tuxedo, you know and whatnot.
When was the first time you heard Charlie Parker?
When he first came here.
With Jay McShann?
Yeah. We had a close relationship, Charlie Parker and, what's the fellow that wrote the book and now the picture is going to come out?
Russell? Ross (inaudible).
Ross, yeah, Dial records. So I was, you know, I was attuned to what was happening when it was happening.
Right. So to you it was just more music, not --
No, it was not defining anything.
Tape 4 begins
Now we can look back, you know, and look at it in a certain way, then, people had a reaction.
Right.
They didn't realize it was a --
Change.
There was an evolution as much as it was a revolution.
Right, but I still say that the wheels of progress--
[end of tape 3, side 2]
